title: Justice for Victims of War Crimes Act
official_summary:
Justice for Victims of War Crimes Act

This act broadens the scope of individuals who are subject to federal prosecution for war crime offenses.

Currently, the federal war crimes statute provides federal jurisdiction over war crime offenses committed anywhere (i.e., inside or outside the United States) if the victim or offender is a member of the Armed Forces or a U.S. national.

First, this act extends federal jurisdiction over war crime offenses committed anywhere to offenses where (1) the victim or offender is an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence; or (2) the offender is present in the United States, regardless of the nationality of the victim or the offender.

Second, the act expands federal jurisdiction over war crime offenses to include offenses that occur in whole or in part within the United States, regardless of whether the victim or offender is a member of the Armed Forces, a U.S. national, or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence.

The act allows an indictment for certain war crime offenses to be instituted any time, making the statute of limitations inapplicable. To undertake a prosecution for war crime offenses, the act requires written certification that prosecution is in the public interest and is necessary to secure substantial justice. The certification is not subject to judicial review.

summary.headline: This law widens federal power to prosecute war crimes by reaching more people and more conduct, and removes the time limit for some of these charges.
summary.what_it_does: The federal war crimes law already covered certain offenses committed anywhere in the world when the victim or offender was a U.S. service member or U.S. national. This act extends federal jurisdiction to cases where the victim or offender is a lawful permanent resident, or where the offender is present in the United States, no matter the nationality of the people involved. It also covers war crime offenses that happen wholly or partly inside the United States, whether or not the people involved are service members, nationals, or permanent residents. For certain war crime charges, an indictment can now be brought at any time, so the statute of limitations does not apply. Prosecutors must also sign a written certification that the case is in the public interest and needed to secure substantial justice, and courts cannot review that certification.

who_it_affects.how: They can now be prosecuted federally for war crime offenses when they are the victim or offender, even if the conduct happened outside the U.S.

who_it_affects.group: Non-U.S. nationals present in the United States
who_it_affects.how: Anyone who is in the U.S. and accused of a covered war crime offense can be prosecuted federally, regardless of their nationality or the victim's.

who_it_affects.group: Anyone accused of war crimes that occur in whole or part within the United States
who_it_affects.how: Conduct inside U.S. territory can be prosecuted federally regardless of whether the people involved are service members or nationals.

who_it_affects.group: Federal prosecutors and the Justice Department
who_it_affects.how: They must provide a written certification that a war crimes prosecution is in the public interest before bringing the case, and that decision cannot be challenged in court.
Some charges can be brought at any time, so cases are not barred by the usual deadline for filing charges.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted January 5, 2023; the summary does not state a separate effective date.
